title: Astrid and the Bell
premise: Pest controller Oscar Joubert takes a routine call to the Vasseur farmhouse, where something leaves human fingerprints in the flour and claw marks in the attic — and he documents everything, because documentation is a kind of prayer. When the village church bell rings one midnight, though it was melted down in 1911, Oscar learns the Vasseurs' dead matriarch left them an inheritance: a debt counted out in bell-rings, each toll claiming a family member's name, memory, and face. As the count climbs toward thirteen, Oscar discovers the thing in the attic is the family's erased ancestor, still ringing for recognition, and that he himself is the uncounted thirteenth — a Vasseur given away at birth. To save the family, Oscar must let the final bell claim his old identity, answering the count with his true name, and the family he found must choose to remember him before the bell falls silent forever.
about_author: Ines Nakamura is a former parish archivist from a small coastal town who spent a decade cataloguing church registries and unclaimed inheritances before turning to fiction. She writes horror about paperwork, family trees, and the things that ring in the dark when records go missing.

chapters.title: The Call-Out
chapters.summary: Oscar Joubert, meticulous pest controller, arrives at the crumbling Vasseur farmhouse to deal with a 'rat problem' and finds flour dusted with human fingerprints too small and too old to be anyone living. He photographs everything, logs times and temperatures, his documentation a private ritual. The emotional beat: unease dressed up as professionalism.

chapters.title: Fingerprints in the Flour
chapters.summary: Oscar sets traps and cameras overnight. The footage shows nothing moving, yet by morning every trap is sprung, empty, and arranged in a neat row — and the fingerprints have multiplied, forming what looks like a tally. He meets the wary Vasseurs: grandmother Yolande, her son Étienne, granddaughter Margaux. Beat: the family knows more than they say.

chapters.title: The House That Keeps Count
chapters.summary: From Margaux's POV, we see the house through a child's eyes: doors that won't stay shut, a cold spot on the stairs shaped like a sitting person, and her grandmother counting under her breath each night. Margaux has started counting too, and the number frightens her. Beat: inherited dread passing down a generation.

chapters.title: What the Registry Says
chapters.summary: Oscar digs into parish archives to trace the farmhouse, finding the Vasseur family tree torn out — a deliberate excision. The 1911 ledger notes the church bell was sold and melted down. The archivist mentions, offhand, that the bell 'never rang right' even before. Beat: documentation reveals a wound, not an answer.

chapters.title: The Bell That Isn't
chapters.summary: At midnight the village church bell rings — a full, bronze peal from a tower that has held no bell for a century. Oscar, awake with his logbook open, records it: eleven tolls. In the morning the village insists no one heard anything. Beat: the private horror of being the only witness.

chapters.title: Yolande's Silence
chapters.summary: Yolande's POV, decades earlier and now: as a girl she watched her mother go silent after the bell rang twelve times, forgetting her own name mid-sentence. Now Yolande keeps the family away from the church and burns letters she can't finish reading. Beat: a survivor who has already lost people to the count.

chapters.title: Étienne Forgets His Coffee
chapters.summary: After the second ringing — twelve tolls — Étienne begins losing small things: the taste of coffee, the name of his dog, the melody he played at his wedding. Oscar's cameras catch him standing in the yard at 3 a.m., facing the church, mouthing numbers. Beat: the count is no longer theoretical.

chapters.title: The Attic Door
chapters.summary: Margaux follows the cold spot upstairs and finds a door that isn't on any blueprint. Behind it: a nursery preserved in dust, a cradle, and a wall covered in tally marks — hundreds, all in the same childish hand. Something in the dark says her name kindly. Beat: the child makes first contact.

chapters.title: Thirteen Names
chapters.summary: Oscar cross-references the tally marks with the mutilated registry and reconstructs the erased name: Aurélien Vasseur, a child recorded born in 1910 and dead in the ledger the same week — no burial, no cause. The bell was melted the following year. He writes the name in his logbook and the ink won't dry. Beat: the mystery gets a face.

chapters.title: What the Bell Was Made Of
chapters.summary: Yolande finally speaks: the 1911 bell was recast from the melted-down farm bell, and the foundry workers swore the new bell rang with a voice not its own. The parish silenced it, and the parish silenced the child with it. 'We paid our debt in silence,' she says. 'It's collecting the interest.' Beat: guilt made structural.

chapters.title: The Third Ringing
chapters.summary: Thirteen tolls at midnight. Margaux wakes with a name in her mouth that isn't hers and writes it on the nursery wall in her sleep: Aurélien. Étienne forgets his daughter's face for a full minute, and the terror of that minute breaks his denial. Beat: the family stops pretending and starts fighting.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: Oscar lays out his evidence to the family — photographs, timestamps, the reconstructed tree — and for the first time treats his logbook as what it has always been: an attempt to make the erased legible. He proposes they answer the bell instead of enduring it. Beat: the plan forms, fragile and human.

chapters.title: The Foundry Ledger
chapters.summary: In the ruined foundry outside town, Oscar finds the casting records: the bell was poured with an offering — coins, a christening gown, and a lock of hair — a folk rite to give the bell a soul. The hair belonged to Aurélien. The bell didn't ring wrong; it rang with a child's voice, and they buried it for it. Beat: horror reframed as grief.

chapters.title: Margaux Goes Upstairs
chapters.summary: Margaux enters the nursery deliberately, bringing her drawings of the family, and leaves them in the cradle. The cold presence sits beside her all night — not menacing, but starving. She tells it, 'You're not a monster. You're just not remembered.' Beat: the child offers what the adults withheld: recognition.

chapters.title: The Bell Answers
chapters.summary: That night the bell rings without being rung — a single, questioning tone, repeated like a child knocking. Yolande, hearing her mother's childhood nickname in the tone, collapses. The entity isn't counting to take; it's counting to be answered. Beat: the rules of the haunting invert.

chapters.title: Étienne's Bargain
chapters.summary: Desperate as his memories erode faster, Étienne tries to end it alone: he breaks into the sealed belfry to destroy the unseen bell's resonance, smashing the empty beam where it hung. The tolling stops — then resumes inside the house itself, in every pipe and pane of glass. Beat: fighting the haunting makes it domestic.

chapters.title: The Thirteenth Name
chapters.summary: The bell rings fourteen times — and Oscar's logbook fills with his own handwriting he doesn't remember making: his birth name, Oscar Vasseur, the thirteenth child of the thirteenth generation, given away before the count could reach him. He has been the uncounted heir all along. Beat: the investigator becomes the inheritance.

chapters.title: What Oscar Forgot
chapters.summary: Yolande's POV: she recognizes the boy she held for one hour in 1974 before her sister took him away. The family's exile from the count depended on his absence; his return completes it. She must confess that her protection was the original erasure. Beat: found family and blood family become the same terrible question.

chapters.title: The Night of the Count
chapters.summary: The final ringing begins — toll after toll through the storm, the house filling with fingerprints, the nursery door standing open. The family gathers in the kitchen, holding hands, and answers each toll aloud with a Vasseur name, refusing to let the count take them silently. Beat: the climax opens with defiance.

chapters.title: Oscar Answers
chapters.summary: At the thirteenth toll, the voice in the walls asks its question at last: who is left? Oscar steps forward and gives his true name — Oscar Vasseur — accepting the count, letting the bell claim the identity he built as armor. The tolling stops mid-swing. In the silence, the fingerprints on the flour spell one word: home. Beat: the climax's sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Empty Belfry
chapters.summary: Morning. The bell is gone — not melted, not hidden, simply finished, and the nursery is warm and ordinary, the tally marks faded to a child's finished sum. Étienne remembers his daughter's face and his wedding melody; Yolande remembers everything, which is its own penance. Margaux leaves one drawing in the cradle: all of them, plus one more. Beat: grief resolving into rest.

chapters.title: Astrid and the Bell
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Oscar — going by a name the family gave him at his one-hour baptism: Astrid, the name his mother whispered and no record kept — stays on at the farmhouse, logbook closed at last. The village church installs a new, honest bell. Some nights Astrid hears a single soft toll, like a child saying goodnight, and does not write it down. Beat: identity chosen, family kept, the haunting at peace.
